author: Athelas Research
title: Royalty Trust Renaissance
text:
Royalty Trust Renaissance
Old Basin, New Development, Unique Asymmetries
Disclosure: The author is long units of CRT, PBT, and SJT. None of this article is financial advice. Please read the full disclaimer here.
My favourite opportunities are those where you can buy a long-term, difficult-to-replace asset trading at distressed prices for short-term reasons. Even better is if this asset has zero marginal cost scaling, perpetual capital compounding, and therefore asymmetric upside.
A well-structured royalty business fits the bill on the latter, yet these rarely trade at distressed prices. The two royalty trusts presented in this article do not exactly represent the latter… at least not yet. But they do appear to represent the former; as being natural gas-focused royalty trusts, they now trade at distressed prices due to poor North American natural gas pricing and structure-inflicted wounds.
Today, North American natural gas is the cheapest molecule of energy found on earth. But once upon a time, the gas-oil ratio was closer to the BTU content ratio (6:1) — a far cry from natural gas’s shale era abundance, which at times has driven the ratio closer to the 20:1-30:1 range. Natural gas is currently widely loathed as an investment, yet change may be in store as it is on the precipice of unprecedented demand growth from both LNG export and power demand buildouts, and infrastructure constraints could slow a supply response. Natural gas prices, at least with a five-year time horizon, appear now to be skewed to the upside.
These natural gas royalty trusts stand to benefit not only from rising commodity prices, driven by inflection points in U.S. power demand growth and LNG exports — but also from 1. new technology revitalizing a century-old basin that is set to lift production, and 2. from the potential for activist investors to push indenture amendments that modernize these outdated structures and unlock massive value currently being squandered by the existing royalty model.
Current natural gas sentiment sits far closer to despair than exuberance; combined with the factors outlined above, this creates what poker players call “multiple outs.”
Background
The year is 1980. Southland Royalty Company had just carved out two new entities that, with their pass-through trust structure, would avoid double taxation of cash flows from oil and gas properties in the San Juan and Permian Basins and distribute royalty income directly to unitholders. At the time, this was quite the entrepreneurial innovation and functioned as a tax-efficient spin-off of these royalty interests. These two trusts exist today as NYSE-listed San Juan Basin Royalty Trust (SJT) and Permian Basin Royalty Trust (PBT). 11 years later, the same team did it again, spinning off some carved-out royalty interests of Cross Timbers Oil Company (later XTO Energy) across New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Texas — IPOing the new entity as Cross Timbers Royalty Trust (CRT) in 1992.
The structure of all three royalty trusts is quite similar. The trusts cannot repurchase or issue new units, cannot purchase or dispose of royalty interests, and have strict requirements around the issuance of debt (only to fund Trust administrative costs). The royalties are structured as net profit interests (NPIs), but in this case, not all the NPIs are created equal. Take SJT, with its pure San Juan Basin, New Mexico exposure; its royalties are structured as 75% NPIs and are calculated as gross proceeds less production costs and capital expenditures. CRT has this type of royalty on properties in Texas and Oklahoma as well, but also features 90% NPIs in NM, TX, and OK, which, although a profit interest in name, are calculated as revenues less costs for property taxes, transportation, and marketing, but importantly do not include production or development costs.
The distinction between the two NPIs is important. These assets were meant to decline over time and pay out royalty cash flows — and that’s that. Vertical dry gas wells were cheap to drill, and therefore the 75% NPI was not overwhelmed by capital expenditures. In the modern age of horizontal drilling, this is no longer the case — and is the primary reason why SJT has not paid a distribution in over two years. In 2024, the operator of San Juan’s properties, Hilcorp, announced it would be spending $34 million to drill two new horizontal wells in the Mancos shale of New Mexico’s San Juan Basin; this was up from 2023 capital spending of just $4.4m. Because of this, “excess production costs” were created on SJT’s end; production costs and capital expenditures swamped royalty revenues, and the distribution needed to be suspended until these excess costs were recovered. Low in-basin natural gas prices have exacerbated the problem, and today SJT still has $7.2m in excess production costs, $999k drawn on its line of credit, and must replenish a $2.0m cash reserve balance before distributions can resume. This is not a good outcome for a trust whose sole purpose is to distribute cash flows to unitholders.
Wrong Structure for Today’s Environment
A good royalty should benefit from inflation through its cost-free exposure to the underlying asset. In the case of oil and gas, it should also benefit from a growing reserve base; producers spend capital to develop a resource, and this capex contributes to future net asset value to the benefit of a royalty owner (who does not have to put up another cent). Throw in the ability to repurchase shares or purchase new royalties, and you have a perpetual capital compounding machine. SJT’s NPIs were great for the San Juan Basin of the past, but with large capital expenditures targeting the Mancos formation, capex that, in a proper structure, would be helping distribution-seeking owners has turned into a nightmare. This structure is largely why the opportunity exists today. Thankfully, as was the case with entrepreneurial individuals setting up these structures in the past, there are also individuals willing to bring these trusts into the modern age.
Playbook for restructuring a royalty business
Texas Pacific Land Corporation (TPL) is a name many will be familiar with. Its long-term performance has been phenomenal, and it shows the compounding power of a well-structured royalty business. Before 2021, TPL was structured as a trust — that was, until activist shareholders Eric Oliver (SoftVest L.P.) and Horizon Kinetics got involved in modernizing TPL. While Texas Pacific’s unique trust structure granted it more flexibility than the three names listed above, it still had significant drawbacks that were ultimately remedied when it converted to a C corp. In May 2026, Oliver took action again, this time seeking to amend the structure of Permian Basin Royalty Trust through a merger with Blackbeard Holding’s US Land Guild. This transaction, if approved, creates an entity similar to TPL and would crucially restructure the Trust’s net profit royalties into 15% revenue royalties and also allow the new C corp to repurchase units and acquire new properties. The new entity will modernize the structure to benefit from a growing reserve base, generate more consistent distributable cash flows, and create a platform for future compounding, while also widening its investable universe to those unable to own Trusts.
It would appear that this type of restructuring is also possible at the smaller but related trusts in SJT and CRT — and this catalyst may be more than just a hunch.
Eric Oliver was purchasing CRT units almost every week from March until the end of June this year; SoftVest now owns over 16% of Cross Timbers. It took around 13% ownership of PBT for Oliver to implement trust amendments and a potential merger there. Over at SJT, Horizon Kinetics holds around 15% of the shares (HK write-up on SJT is a must-read).
The merger with USLG is a key part of the PBT-SoftVest playbook, and a merger would likely need to be part of any value-unlocking transformation at CRT or SJT — especially given their small size. Hilcorp is the main operator for both SJT and CRT’s New Mexico properties and would likely need to be involved in any deal, while Argent Trust Company is the trustee for SJT, CRT, and PBT. I am speculating here, but given these significant overlaps and the common interest of SJT and CRT’s major unit holders in modernizing the structures and the adjacent land positions (see maps below), it would make a lot of sense to combine CRT and SJT in some form. Who knows what will happen, but that would be quite an intriguing combination!
Mancos Shale: Reviving the San Juan
While amending the trusts is an interesting dynamic, it is but a pillar of the thesis for these natural gas royalty trusts. One of the “outs,” if you will. For now, the value lies in what is under the ground —potentially 20 Tcf of dry gas in the largely untapped Mancos Shale.
The San Juan Basin of northwestern New Mexico is one of the largest and oldest producing dry gas basins in the United States and has produced >42.6 Tcf over its life. But since the early 2000s, when it produced 4.5 Bcf/day, it has been a basin in decline. In recent years, oil majors like ConocoPhillips and BP have exited the basin to target hotter plays in the Permian. Smaller private firms filled the void, and Hilcorp (Jeffrey Hildebrand), LOGOS Energy and Mach Natural Resources (Tom Ward of SandRidge, Chesapeake fame) have entered the basin in a large way, targeting the prolific Mancos Shale. LOGOS in particular has drilled some incredible dry gas wells in Rio Arriba County, per a January 2026 press release:
FARMINGTON, N.M., Jan. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LOGOS Energy, LLC (”LOGOS”, or, the “Company”) announced record-breaking results from its 2025 Mancos Shale development program in the San Juan Basin, highlighting continued operational excellence and production growth.
Since the 2022 management-led buyout with North Hudson Resource Partners, LOGOS’ operated production has tripled and the company has drilled 28 of the top 36 producing wells in San Juan Basin history ranked by peak monthly production.
The Company’s Rosa Unit 756H achieved a Peak IP30 of 26.6 MMcfe/d from 13,721’ of completed lateral, the highest 30-day rate ever recorded in the Basin. This milestone follows the Rosa Unit 704H, brought online in 2024, which reached 25.5 MMcfe/d from 13,363’ of completed lateral.
Clearly the gas is there, but natural gas is far from sexy right now, and the basin’s recent successes have been overshadowed by more glamorous oily areas like the Permian. The Mancos Shale enables the San Juan Basin to grow once again. TPL and PBT show what can happen if both production and pricing on royalty assets improve. Higher natural gas prices lead to more drilling and production by the operators; every dollar put towards future production is an investment which supports the net-asset-value of the royalty trusts. These trusts currently cannot issue new units, meaning production growth translates directly to production per unit growth and, if margins remain stable, then growth in distributable income per unit. Below is an example of the Carracas Gas Field in Rio Arriba County, New Mexico from 1953-2023. You can see how one property can be transformed by recompletions, infill drilling, and new technologies like horizontal drilling that all enhance recovery of the resource and drive the underlying asset’s net asset value (this field was divested in 2000 for $19 million and then again in 2014 for $225 million).
San Juan Basin Royalty Trust has just one conveyance with properties across San Juan and Rio Arriba Counties in New Mexico. Cross Timbers has five separate conveyances held by the trust. All five of CRT’s conveyances are independent, and excess production costs on one do not prohibit other conveyances from paying distributions.
SJT’s basin-wide royalty package grants it greater exposure to new wells being drilled on its land; the largest risk for SJT is that capex spent on the Mancos continues to swamp proceeds — a Hugoton Royalty Trust outcome is not totally out of the picture here, and this risk needs to be appreciated. CRT is largely protected in this respect due to their cost-free royalty structure in New Mexico, and while their Mancos exposure is less than San Juan’s, it could still be a factor in future production. While production is a key element, the price one receives for their resource is also crucial to inflecting distributions.
A Brighter Future for Gas Pricing?
My view is that over the mid-to-long term, natural gas price movements are skewed to the upside. Demand growth over the next five years seems unprecedented; U.S. electricity consumption is growing for the first time since the early 2000s, and LNG projects coming online will only continue to draw multiple new Bcf/day leading into 2030. This could quickly shift a volatile, oversupplied gas market into a deficit.
There is debate about how quickly future supply will be able to react — this lag has historically resulted in spikes in the price (and is what drives a cycle). My focus is almost always on supply when analyzing a capital cycle; with natural gas, a factor to consider is that there may be infrastructure constraints and an inability of fracking/drilling units to keep up with surging demand requirements in the coming years.
In general, the supply side is more reliably calculated than future demand, but in today’s natural gas market, supply changes feel tougher to clock. What I do know is that human psychology in business cycles is timeless. Most will rush to deploy capital in a space when it feels good. Very few have the stomach to invest when it feels risky — yet when it feels worst is likely the near-optimal time to get interested. Natural gas feels like it’s much closer to the latter than the former.
Trust convexity to natural gas pricing
The positive skew I see for natural gas prices over the next five years, combined with depressed unit prices, makes SJT and CRT intriguing, especially given their strong dependence on gas pricing (~97% of SJT and ~2/3rds of CRT revenues are attributable to natural gas). SJT’s distributions historically (pre-suspension) have a ~94% correlation with realized natural gas prices. While this is excellent when prices cover costs (production costs average ~$1.60/Mcf since 1Q24), and distributions can be made, it also means that when prices drop, the distribution suffers. SJT is currently about $10.2m short of being able to resume distributions; modelling with $2.50/Mcf gas prices, I conservatively estimate distributions will resume in the middle of 2028. At face value, not great. Yet this is assuming annual average capex of $14m for 2026-2028; $13.55m is guided by Hilcorp for 2026, down from $14m, but at current gas prices this is likely to be further reduced in 2027/28 (see chart below for how unprecedented the current capex spend is).
There is risk, but there is also massive convexity to gas prices, and the convexity of SJT’s distributions to natural gas prices is really incredible. Below $2/Mcf gas, SJT struggles and risks running into issues with their line of credit; at $2.50/Mcf it slowly recovers, but at $3.50/Mcf natural gas starting in 3Q26, even assuming the flat capex above and flat production, distributions could resume as early as 1Q27, and at a $2.50 unit price, the 2027 distribution yield would be ~22% on cost. In the past decade (a rather weak one for energy prices), SJT has paid out $5.51 in distributions per unit, despite zero payout for the past two years.
For Cross Timbers, the three 90% NPIs in NM, TX, and OK are the cash cows of the trust — their distribution power ebbs and flows with commodity prices but should provide positive distributions regardless of capital expenditures or commodity pricing. Two of CRT’s conveyances are similar to SJT’s 75% NPI and are currently underwater on excess production costs but represent only a 10% share of attributable reserves. CRT’s excess production cost conveyances, however, are largely oil weighted, and oil prices have improved markedly in recent months. If these 75% NPI’s, which are essentially dormant assets, inflect back into the black, they could become a nice contributor to distribution power.
With their convexity to commodity pricing, the unique and difficult-to-replace assets held by Cross Timbers and San Juan stand to benefit from improving oil and gas prices.
Risks
Permanent loss of capital is the ultimate risk in any capital allocation decision. San Juan Royalty Trust, while offering greater upside in an optimistic scenario, also faces the risk of future capital impairment. My math suggests SJT needs in-basin gas prices to average ~$2.87/Mcf for 2H2026 and 1Q2027 to bring the excess costs down to zero and begin making a dent in the line of credit by the end of the first quarter (again assuming the full Hilcorp budget is spent and ~$1.6/Mcf production costs) — with winter months still ahead and strong heating demand in July/August, this is not far-fetched but definitely not a slam dunk (note, El Paso San Juan gas is currently over $3, and at a premium to Henry Hub). I prefer CRT because it holds much less risk of near-term permanent capital loss given the structure of the 90% NPIs versus the 75% NPI held by SJT. There is simply more staying power with the 90% NPI structure. In general, the key risks I see are:
Lower-for-longer natural gas prices: SJT continues to draw on its line of credit and death spirals under the burden of excess production costs — Hugoton-style. Currently, $1m is drawn on its $2m line of credit. In recent months, they have been drawing at ~$50k per month.
Operators could theoretically abuse 75% NPIs until the unit price hits zero. For SJT, Hilcorp could drive the unit price to zero through capex spending and then purchase for next to nothing in a liquidation scenario.
Poor performance of underlying properties: Hilcorp's recent horizontal wells (culprit of the excess production costs) created a short-lived bump in production and appear underwhelming for their cost.
Catalysts
Trust restructuring and converting the NPIs to revenue royalties would be a dream scenario for both trusts. If done properly, this restructuring could be an incentive to develop royalty-held properties. A cost-free royalty on vast and prolific natural resource deposits would be an incredible real asset, capital-light business that should benefit for years to come (an interesting
X threadtouched on this point back in 2024). This scenario is the power-law upside.Continued field development on royalty properties. Particularly in the emerging Mancos Shale play.
Commodity prices improving.
Resumption of distributions at SJT should trigger a rerating as it effectively converts from a short-dated call-option-type instrument to a long-duration call option with a yield.

Thank you for reading.

summary: Low in-basin natural gas prices have exacerbated the problem, and today SJT still has $7.2m in excess production costs, $999k drawn on its line of credit, and must replenish a $2.0m cash reserve balance before distributions can resume. SJT’s NPIs were great for the San Juan Basin of the past, but with large capital expenditures targeting the Mancos formation, capex that, in a proper structure, would be helping distribution-seeking owners has turned into a nightmare.
